extracted.intended_audience: graduate students in mathematics preparing papers, theses, quizzes, or tests
extracted.subtask_description: Guide for composing mathematical articles and theses using LaTeX/AMS-LaTeX: document structure, proclamations (theorems/definitions), math displays, tables/matrices, referencing, macros, and typesetting workflow. Emphasizes best practices for graduate students and thesis formatting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document structure (preamble and body)
rubrics_metrics.description: The source file of a LaTeX document has an extension .tex and is divided into several parts including a preamble and a body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put formatting commands, package loading, custom definitions, and \\newtheorem declarations in the preamble; the body contains top matter (title, author, abstract), main matter (sections, chapters, subsections, appendices) and back matter (bibliography). For large documents split into separate .tex files and include them (\include) rather than create one big file. Example skeleton with \documentclass{article} and typical preamble shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use current LaTeX version and appropriate document class
rubrics_metrics.description: This article assumes LaTeX 2e; many commands (e.g., \documentclass{...}) do not apply to older LaTeX 2.09.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the correct document class (article, report, elsart, kapproc, etc.) and the publisher/journal's style file when submitting. Do not mix incompatible formats; ensure the typesetter in your environment (e.g., PCTeX32) is set to LaTeX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Load appropriate packages in the preamble
rubrics_metrics.description: Load packages as needed, e.g. \usepackage{amsmath}, \usepackage{amssymb}, \usepackage{amsthm}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: amsmath provides align, multline, split, gather, etc.; amssymb provides blackboard bold and many symbols; amsthm provides theorem/proof environments and styles. Put \usepackage commands between \documentclass and \begin{document}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble: custom definitions and macros
rubrics_metrics.description: Define custom commands and environments in the preamble using \def or \newcommand and \newtheorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Examples: \def eq{ egin{equation}}, 
ewcommand{\Id}{{ f 1}}, 
ewtheorem{lemma}{Lemma}. Keep macro names clear and consistent; optional arguments for 
ewcommand (e.g., 
ewcommand{\NewSum}[1][n]{...}) can save typing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typesetting workflow and error handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Typeset the .tex file (e.g., press Typeset in PCTeX32); typesetting may create .aux and .log files and may require multiple runs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run LaTeX repeatedly until labels and references are correct. Inspect .log for errors; PCTeX32 can jump to error locations. If typesetting stops, fix the source and re-run. Ignore .aux and usually .log unless errors are reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use templates or existing skeleton files
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ready-made templates from your LaTeX distribution or copy an existing .tex skeleton (e.g., Thesis.tex) rather than starting from scratch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Templates already include necessary parts for theses or articles and conform to institutional requirements; modify content rather than format commands in provided thesis skeletons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not modify thesis-specific formatting commands
rubrics_metrics.description: When working with a provided Thesis.tex (or institutional style), do not modify formatting commands that enforce Graduate School requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only edit content; changing margin/formatting commands in the thesis template may violate requirements. Use templates for quizzes or tests where formatting edits are acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page layout via preamble length commands
rubrics_metrics.description: Set margins and text area using \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{...}, \setlength{\textwidth}{...}, \setlength{\topmargin}{...}, \setlength{\textheight}{...}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute resulting margins (examples given). Prefer Page Format Template from PCTeX32 rather than ad-hoc changes. Understand default values (1 inch) when adjusting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proclamations (theorems, definitions, lemmas) via \newtheorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Proclamations in LaTeX (theorem, proposition, lemma, definition, corollary, example, remark) must be defined in the preamble with \newtheorem and invoked as environments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: \newtheorem{theorem}{Theorem}. Use labels (\label{T:set1}) to reference proclamations. You may number proclamations consecutively, within sections, or separately by using different counters. Use \newtheorem* to define unnumbered named proclamations (e.g., Main Theorem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem styles with amsthm
rubrics_metrics.description: amsthm provides three styles for proclamations: plain (default, most emphatic), definition (less emphatic), and remark (least emphatic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set the style in the preamble using \theoremstyle{plain|definition|remark}. Choose appropriate style to reflect emphasis of a proclamation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof environment usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use \begin{proof} ... \end{proof} from amsthm for proofs; optional argument customizes the heading (e.g., [Uniqueness], [Proof of Theorem~\ref{...}]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a proof ends with a displayed equation rather than text, omit the q.e.d. symbol by redefining \qedsymbol or using \renewcommand{\qedsymbol}{}. Use optional argument to refer to the theorem being proved if the proof is not immediately after the theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer displayed math for long/complicated expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Long or complicated mathematical expressions should be displayed rather than inline to improve readability and spacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inline math uses single $...$; display math uses $$...$$ or environments like equation, align, multline. Use \mathsurround in the preamble to control inline math spacing if needed (example: \mathsurround 1.5pt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Control spacing within mathematical formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: LaTeX has predefined spacing commands for math: \, \:, \;, \quad, \qquad and \hspace{...}; use \mbox{...} to insert text in math mode and \phantom to reserve width.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert small horizontal spaces (\,) where needed for better appearance. Use \boxed{...} to highlight important formulas. Be careful placing punctuation inside math environments to avoid unwanted gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling, referencing, and citing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use \label{...} to label sections, equations, theorems, etc., and \ref{...} to refer to them. Use \cite{...} to cite bibliography entries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use label prefixes like eq:, def:, T: or App: for counters (convention but optional). Labels must be unique, cannot start with a space, and cannot contain commas. Run LaTeX multiple times to resolve references; mistyped labels produce question marks or (??). Use \cite[pages~2--12]{...} to cite pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate displayed-math environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Different environments serve different formatting needs: equation, array, align, align*, gather, gather*, multline, split, pmatrix, array, tabular, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use align (amsmath) and & alignment markers to line up equals signs; use \notag to suppress numbering on particular lines; choose align vs align* depending on whether you want numbering per line. Use multline or split for long expressions to get a single equation number. gather* centers displays without numbering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrays and matrices formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: array environment (with {l,c,r} and vertical bars |) creates aligned columns; pmatrix, bmatrix, etc., from amsmath create matrices with delimiters automatically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select column specifiers (r, c, l) carefully — use rr for numbers with signs to align correctly. Use vertical bars in the column spec (e.g., {cc|c}) to create vertical lines. Prefer pmatrix for simpler matrix input and array when custom layout or vertical bars are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tables: tabular and array usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use tabular for complex tables; array for arranging math in displays; control column spans with \multicolumn and reduce font size with environments like \begin{small}...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use \hline and custom \Hline for thicker lines; adjust vertical spacing with \[...ex] after \\ ; use \multicolumn{...}{c|}{...} to span columns; example provided for a 12-column schedule table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Macro hygiene and reuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Define custom commands (\newcommand, \def) for frequently used notations and for clarity, including commands that take optional and multiple arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: \newcommand{\reversion}[1]{#1 \, \tilde{}}, \newcommand{\NewSum}[1][n]{...}. Macros can take up to nine parameters; the first parameter may be optional. Use meaningful macro names and document them in the preamble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness and conventions for labels and bibliography keys
rubrics_metrics.description: Labels and \bibitem keys should follow consistent conventions (e.g., last name + year) and must be unique; keys cannot start with spaces or contain commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: \bibitem{hahn1993}, \cite{hahn1993,gratzer1999} yields [2,4]. Use the argument to \begin{thebibliography}{9} to indicate the widest label width (9, 99, 999) so numbering formats properly.

rubrics_metrics.name: AMS bibliography formatting conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: In AMS style references, only titles are emphasized and volume numbers are set in boldface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the AMS examples for formatting authors, titles, journal, year, volume, and pages. Use thebibliography environment for manual entries or use BibTeX if available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appendices and appendix labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Use \appendix to switch to appendix sections; subsequent \section commands produce appendix titles (A, B, ...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label appendices (e.g., \label{App:fw}) and refer to them via \ref{App:fw}. Consider using a distinct label prefix (App) for appendix counters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary document truncation for editing
rubrics_metrics.description: It can be convenient to insert a macro (e.g., \newcommand{\ed}{\end{document}}) and use it in the body to stop typesetting early during edits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place \ed where you wish to temporarily stop typesetting; remove or comment it out (%) when ready to typeset the whole document. Useful when working on a small part of a large document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize readability and visual appearance of formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust horizontal/vertical spacing, alignment, and environment choice to improve the visual appearance of equations and matrices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: use \\[0.5ex] to add vertical space between array rows; use \,, \quad, \qquad for horizontal spacing; choose centering vs right/left alignment for matrix columns depending on sign widths; use \boxed to highlight key results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know which features require amsmath/amsthm/amssymb
rubrics_metrics.description: Many advanced environments and symbols are not part of standard LaTeX and require specific AMS packages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Load amsmath for align, multline, split, gather, pmatrix; amsthm for proof/theorem styles; amssymb for blackboard bold and additional symbols. Explicitly state in the preamble which packages are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of editor/tools to navigate typesetting errors
rubrics_metrics.description: When typesetting errors occur, the editor/LaTeX front-end (e.g., PCTeX32) will report line numbers and can open the editor with the cursor at the error location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cancel or resume typesetting as appropriate; inspect .log for details if needed. Often the error can be fixed without reading the entire .log.
